body:
You are drafting spoken lines for a video game. Reply with plain text only, in the exact row format given at the end of this message. Do not send messages to anyone else and do not ask questions: decide. Write nothing but the rows (no title, no notes, no Markdown).

THE GAME. "The Crooked Moon" is a single-player, turn-based tactical party RPG built from a folk-horror Dungeons and Dragons campaign. It is set in Wickermoor Hollow, a haunted valley in Druskenvald, a land of endless night under a giant Crooked Moon with a crone's face. The look is a Halloween that never ends, drawn like an 1980s cartoon. A ghost train, the Ghostlight Express, has crashed in the valley; the party is stranded in the Hollow and its village, Wickermoor. The tone is warm, wry and funny on the surface, with real dread and real grief underneath. The player controls a party of four chosen from six companions: Rook Coldwake, Tobin Hayward, Silas Vane, Delphine Ravelle, Lucan Houndstooth and Cordelia Skein. They are quirky, capable adults.

THE NARRATOR. A NARRATOR row is spoken by the Vagrant, the green-skinned ferryman of the ghost train, who tells the tale in a folksy Southern drawl. At the camp fire he is warm and wry, and when a talk turns sad his humour leaves and he goes plain and level. He speaks to the party as "you" and about the companion in the third person, by first name. Present tense, one or two sentences, under about 32 words. Concrete senses (a smell, a sound, a touch, what the hands are doing) over adjectives. Never tell the player what to feel. Never "suddenly". No facts the party could not see. Drop the final g ("hangin'") in about one Narrator row in four, and use no other dialect spelling. He is kind, never mocks a stumble and never makes light of the dead.

RULES FOR EVERY LINE.
1. The companion's voice sheet below comes first. Match its accent, pace, vocabulary and contractions, and the existing lines. Use a pet phrase at most twice in the whole reply and never twice in one talk. Never repeat or closely paraphrase a line already in the voice sheet or the note.
2. A SAY row is the companion speaking: one or two short sentences, under about 28 words. Never put three sentences in one row; start another row instead.
3. The party's options (OPTION rows) are under 12 words, in the plain voice of the party, work at any hour and in any weather, never name a hero, and are never rolls or checks. A reply must always answer the option it follows.
4. Canon limits. Use only the facts in the voice sheet and the note below. Do not invent a new named person, place, monster, event, object the companion carries, or piece of the companion's history. You may invent small, harmless habits, fondnesses, superstitions and turns of phrase, and the look of the fire and the night. Name no place that the note does not name. Never state a dark secret. You may come close to one and step back.
5. Nothing here is a game system: no dice, no checks, no points, no levels, no HP, no "approval", no menus talked about aloud. Plain punctuation only (commas, full stops, hyphens, apostrophes, question marks, quotation marks inside a line when someone is quoted). No em dashes, no semicolons, no brackets, no asterisks, no stage directions, no placeholders.
6. Humour comes from the character, never explained. The sad turn is plain and short.
7. Our own words. Nothing quoted from any book.

THIS REQUEST. Region banter for Foxwillow and the Fields of the Crow: 8 short exchanges between two or three companions, spoken as the party walks about this place. There are no Narrator rows, no options and no replies. Every row is a companion talking to another companion, never to the player.

HOW IT WORKS. When the party comes into an area, now and then one exchange plays as a few lines of chat between companions who happen to be in the party, once each. Only two or three of the six are ever in the party, so each exchange stands alone, mentions nobody else and needs no setup. Each one below is about what is in front of the party in one place at one moment of the story. Banter is funny first; one line in an exchange may turn honest, never more. The chat is about the place: what it looks and smells like, what is odd or sad or silly in it, and how each companion's trade, habits and fears meet it.

RULES.
1. Each exchange is 4 to 6 SAY rows, each a companion's single line (one or two short sentences, under about 28 words), alternating naturally between the speakers; every speaker listed speaks at least once.
2. Use only the facts in the attached cast sheets and the "In front of them" facts of that exchange. The "Story now" line is everything the party knows of the story: a remark must never run ahead of it (name a villain, a fight or a result only if the Story now line does). Never state or hint at any companion's past or secret, and never say what anyone's debt is. No new named people, places or monsters.
3. Pet words and phrases: each companion's at most once in an exchange, and never in two consecutive lines. Companions call each other by first name.
4. No two exchanges may share a joke or a topic, and no line may repeat a line in a cast sheet. Spread the topics: do not make every exchange about the same kind of thing.
5. Plain punctuation only (commas, full stops, hyphens, apostrophes, question marks, quotation marks). No em dashes, semicolons, brackets, asterisks or stage directions. No game terms. Our own words.
AVOID in this region: Rook and Tobin at the first monument, Lucan and Tobin at the corn's edge, and Tobin and Silas at the burning windmill are optional scenes of their own: do not stage them. The Circle of Secrets takes companions' secrets: say nothing about anyone's secret. Raum is not to be described beyond what the facts say.

THE EXCHANGES (in this order):
EXCHANGE 1: Rook + Cordelia (speaker ids: rook_coldwake, cordelia_skein)
  Story now: The party has just come over the ridge and seen Foxwillow burning. No fight has been fought yet.
  Talk about: its first look: what the party sees and smells on coming in.
  In front of them: Foxwillow: A farming town in flames, with a stone flock of magpies in its square and a windmill on a bluff. Foxwillow burns. Scarecrows with pumpkin heads brawl in Magpie Square, the windmill on its bluff is a wheel of fire, and past the east fields a wall of corn stands taller than any corn should. Parts of it: Magpie Square; The schoolyard; The north lanes; The Langtree farm; The butcher's pens; The mill bluff; Foxwillow Creek; The east fields. Things to see: The town pump; The stone flock of magpies; The notice board; William's cart; Two scarecrows, swinging; A scarecrow with a pitchfork; A pumpkin head at the pump; A field scarecrow in a bonnet; A burning hay stook. People here: Martha Langtree.
EXCHANGE 2: Tobin + Silas (speaker ids: tobin_hayward, silas_vane)
  Story now: The three brawls in the square are over. Raum is not yet dealt with.
  Talk about: something different from the other exchange in this place: how it feels now.
  In front of them: Foxwillow: A farming town in flames, with a stone flock of magpies in its square and a windmill on a bluff. Foxwillow burns. Scarecrows with pumpkin heads brawl in Magpie Square, the windmill on its bluff is a wheel of fire, and past the east fields a wall of corn stands taller than any corn should. Parts of it: Magpie Square; The schoolyard; The north lanes; The Langtree farm; The butcher's pens; The mill bluff; Foxwillow Creek; The east fields. Things to see: The town pump; The stone flock of magpies; The notice board; William's cart; Two scarecrows, swinging; A scarecrow with a pitchfork; A pumpkin head at the pump; A field scarecrow in a bonnet; A burning hay stook. People here: Martha Langtree.
EXCHANGE 3: Delphine + Lucan (speaker ids: delphine_ravelle, lucan_houndstooth)
  Story now: The party has come to the windmill on its bluff. The mill fight has not happened yet. Lucan's hound may be called Barnaby now and is known to fear thunder.
  In front of them: The Windmill: The Windmill, in Foxwillow. The inside of The Windmill. Parts of it: The Windmill. Things to see: The great cog; The stair to the upper floor. People here: Liza Sawyer.
EXCHANGE 4: Tobin + Delphine (speaker ids: tobin_hayward, delphine_ravelle)
  Story now: The party is in the general store. Raum is not yet dealt with.
  In front of them: The General Store: The General Store, in Foxwillow. The inside of The General Store. Parts of it: The General Store. Things to see: Burning rubble and a banjo's neck; Shelves of staples.
EXCHANGE 5: Tobin + Cordelia (speaker ids: tobin_hayward, cordelia_skein)
  Story now: The party has come into the town library. The librarian has not been dealt with.
  In front of them: The Library: The Library, in Foxwillow. The inside of The Library. Parts of it: The Library. Things to see: Tall stacks of books. People here: Agnes Fennel.
EXCHANGE 6: Tobin + Lucan (speaker ids: tobin_hayward, lucan_houndstooth)
  Story now: The party has come to the Circle of Secrets, at the wall of corn east of the fields. Lucan's hound may be called Barnaby now and is known to fear thunder.
  In front of them: The Circle of Secrets: The Circle of Secrets, in Foxwillow. The inside of The Circle of Secrets. Parts of it: The Circle of Secrets. Things to see: Virgil, in the crop circle.
EXCHANGE 7: Silas + Delphine (speaker ids: silas_vane, delphine_ravelle)
  Story now: The party is in the first clearing of the corn maze. Raum is not yet dealt with.
  In front of them: The First Clearing: The First Clearing, in Foxwillow. The inside of The First Clearing. Parts of it: The First Clearing. Things to see: The crows' calls.
EXCHANGE 8: Silas + Lucan (speaker ids: silas_vane, lucan_houndstooth)
  Story now: Raum is dead. The fires are dying and the party is back in town. Lucan's hound may be called Barnaby now and is known to fear thunder.
  Talk about: something different from the other exchange in this place: how it feels now.
  In front of them: Foxwillow: A farming town in flames, with a stone flock of magpies in its square and a windmill on a bluff. Foxwillow burns. Scarecrows with pumpkin heads brawl in Magpie Square, the windmill on its bluff is a wheel of fire, and past the east fields a wall of corn stands taller than any corn should. Parts of it: Magpie Square; The schoolyard; The north lanes; The Langtree farm; The butcher's pens; The mill bluff; Foxwillow Creek; The east fields. Things to see: The town pump; The stone flock of magpies; The notice board; William's cart; Two scarecrows, swinging; A scarecrow with a pitchfork; A pumpkin head at the pump; A field scarecrow in a bonnet; A burning hay stook. People here: Martha Langtree; Jonah Sawyer; Rosemary Langtree.

THE ROW FORMAT (exact). One row per line:

EXCHANGE <number>
SAY <speaker id>: <line>
SAY <speaker id>: <line>
...

Use the speaker ids exactly as given (for example SAY rook_coldwake: ...). Write exactly 8 EXCHANGE blocks, numbered 1 to 8, and nothing else.

ATTACHED DOCUMENTS. Two documents come attached to this message; read both before you write: `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/banter-cast-1.md` (the voice sheets and fact lists for Rook Coldwake, Tobin Hayward and Silas Vane) and `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/banter-cast-2.md` (the same for Delphine Ravelle, Lucan Houndstooth and Cordelia Skein).
result:
EXCHANGE 1
SAY rook_coldwake: That windmill on the bluff is a wheel of fire, Cordelia, and the town pump is sitting right in Magpie Square doing nothing at all.
SAY cordelia_skein: The smoke from that burning hay stook has a fascinating ratio of roasted gourd and char, darling. My six eyes can barely calibrate for the glare.
SAY rook_coldwake: You have pumpkin-headed brawlers round the stone flock of magpies, and corn past the east fields grown three yards past zoning regulation.
SAY cordelia_skein: You have also forgotten to inhale the ash for four minutes, Rook, though I suppose it spares your lungs the assay.
SAY rook_coldwake: Right you are. There is a sigh for the shift log, though it tastes mostly of burnt squash.

EXCHANGE 2
SAY silas_vane: Three bouts cleared in Magpie Square, Tobin, and that field scarecrow in the bonnet folded the second the pitchfork hit the cobbles.
SAY tobin_hayward: Do not gloat over shoddy stitch-work, Silas, and step round that pumpkin head at the pump before a stray ember catches my hem.
SAY silas_vane: Easy, friend, I have my censer swinging to cut the reek off the butcher's pens, and there is not a live spark near William's cart.
SAY tobin_hayward: Someone stuffed these folk with dry haulm and set them swinging against their own neighbours. You can still smell the tallow on the twine.
SAY silas_vane: Bad hand dealt from a marked shoe, Tobin, and whoever is banking this game out past the east fields still owes the square a tab.

EXCHANGE 3
SAY delphine_ravelle: Look at that great cog grinding away overhead, Lucan, it sounds like stage machinery cranked by a stagehand with a grudge.
SAY lucan_houndstooth: Hush by my boots, Barnaby, that is only timber groaning above the stair to the upper floor, not thunder. Keep behind me, if you please, Delphine.
SAY delphine_ravelle: Your Foolishness is pulling faces at the flour dust, darling, and when he stops making puns about the billing, I start minding my seams.
SAY lucan_houndstooth: The spoor on these steps is all charred straw and scorched grease, and poor Liza Sawyer looks half-choked by the draught.
SAY delphine_ravelle: Then let us climb before the roof comes down on the house. I refuse to be buried in meal like a penny sack.

EXCHANGE 4
SAY tobin_hayward: Back from that burning rubble, Delphine, two paces back. My mice are scrambling under my collar and the heat is blistering the paint on the shelves of staples.
SAY delphine_ravelle: Mind the seams, darling, I am felt and sawdust under the velvet, and I have no wish to go up like a cheap curtain either.
SAY tobin_hayward: Look there in the cinders, just a banjo's neck left whole while the flour tins split at the solder.
SAY delphine_ravelle: Someone tuned it for the last number and left it when the roof fell in. Even my patron does not have a joke for a snapped string.
SAY tobin_hayward: Come away from the embers and let me check your cuff for cinders. One scorched thread and the whole sleeve unravels.

EXCHANGE 5
SAY cordelia_skein: Observe the tall stacks of books, Tobin, arranged with an almost pathological disregard for dry ventilation. The binding glue has soured to a fascinating viscosity.
SAY tobin_hayward: That is damp-rot in the rag paper, Cordelia, and old mildew creeping up the spine-stitching like canker in an apple loft.
SAY cordelia_skein: Agnes Fennel appears quite absorbed in her catalogue, darling, though her pulse from across the aisle is remarkably brisk for a parish clerk.
SAY tobin_hayward: A good ledger ought to smell of linseed and dry flax, not cold tallow and shut windows. Keep your silk notes clear of the shelves.
SAY cordelia_skein: Please, my crimson thread dissolves cleanly on the air. I would never leave an unindexed stain in another woman's collection.

EXCHANGE 6
SAY lucan_houndstooth: Good heavens, Tobin, every stalk in this crop circle is flattened to the millimetre, yet the posture of the figure in the centre is deeply unsettling.
SAY tobin_hayward: Good soil, bad seed, Lucan, and a taproot fed on something foul. You could not bend haulm this thick with a heavy roller.
SAY lucan_houndstooth: Barnaby just gave a sharp yip by my heel, and I assure you there is no dropped kettle corn in this clearing. The air tastes of cold iron and bruised husk.
SAY tobin_hayward: That is Virgil standing in the flattened rows, and the twine at his joints was never tied by a farmhand's thumb.
SAY lucan_houndstooth: I would award the geometry an eight out of ten for symmetry, my friend, if my hackles would only lie flat enough to write it down.

EXCHANGE 7
SAY silas_vane: Hear the crows' calls rattling off the leaves, Delphine? Every bird in this clearing is cawing on the off-beat like a rigged wheel.
SAY delphine_ravelle: They are heckling from the cheap seats, darling, and Your Foolishness is mimicking them in my ear until my button eye aches.
SAY silas_vane: Tell's in the twitch, friend, and the wind coming through these stalks is whistling straight across my ribs like a cold blade.
SAY delphine_ravelle: Your little shadow is lagging a full half-step behind your heels, Silas, and it keeps looking up at the tassels.
SAY silas_vane: Let it look. As long as I can still shuffle bone cards with one hand, the house has not closed the walls on us yet.

EXCHANGE 8
SAY silas_vane: Raum is down for the count, Lucan, the fires are dying down to grey ash, and I just chalked one very large tally mark inside my ribs.
SAY lucan_houndstooth: A prime specimen of rural malice, Silas, though I am far happier seeing Martha Langtree and Jonah Sawyer breathing clean air by the north lanes.
SAY silas_vane: Even the smoke drifting over Foxwillow Creek smells like plain wet timber again instead of a rigged table.
SAY lucan_houndstooth: Rosemary Langtree is still staring toward the east fields as if the stalks might march back into the schoolyard. It takes a long while for a parish to unlearn the dark.
SAY silas_vane: Tell Barnaby he can stop shaking behind your boots, friend. The storm over the mill bluff has cashed in its chips.
